'''Peter Gray''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]]<ref name=frs/> (25 August 1926 – 7 June 2012) was Professor of [[Physical Chemistry]] at the [[University of Leeds]] and subsequently [[Master (college)|Master]] of [[Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge]].<ref name="obituary">Professor Stephen Scott. [http://www.leeds.ac.uk/secretariat/obituaries/2012/gray_peter.html Professor Peter Gray, DSc, FRSC, FRS]. University of Leeds/secretariat/obituaries/</ref><ref>{{Citation
| last1  = Gray
| first1 = P.
| last2  = Scott
| first2 = S. K.
| name-list-style = amp
| title     = Chemical Oscillations and Instabilities Non-linear Chemical Kinetics
| publisher = Clarendon Press
| date    = 12 May 1994
}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Gray attended [[Newport High School, Bettws Lane|Newport High School]].<ref name="combustion">John Griffiths. [http://www.combustion.org.uk/newsletter/newsletteroct06/gray.html COMBUSTION PEOPLE Professor Peter Gray, FRS: 80 this year!] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130109090353/http://www.combustion.org.uk/newsletter/newsletteroct06/gray.html |date=9 January 2013 }}</ref> Gray was educated at the [[University of Cambridge]] where he was awarded a Bachelor of Arts in [[Natural Sciences (Cambridge)|Natural Sciences]] in 1946 and a PhD in [[Chemistry]] three years later.{{citation needed|date=September 2014}}

==Career==
In 1955 Gray was appointed a lecturer in [[Chemistry]] at the [[University of Leeds]].  He was promoted to [[Reader (academic rank)|Reader]] in 1959 and to a personal chair as Professor of [[Physical Chemistry]] in 1962.  He became Head of the Department of [[Physical Chemistry]] on the resignation of [[Frederick Dainton, Baron Dainton|Professor Lord Dainton]] in 1965.  His research interests included combustion flame and explosion [[oscillatory]] reactions and [[Chaos theory|chaos in chemistry]].<ref name="caius" />

Gray left [[University of Leeds|Leeds]] when he was elected [[Master (college)|Master]] of his old college [[Gonville and Caius College]], Cambridge in 1988.<ref name="University of Leeds, Obituary">[http://www.leeds.ac.uk/secretariat/obituaries/2012/gray_peter.html University of Leeds, Obituary]</ref> He remained [[Master (college)|Master]] until 1996 and was then a [[Fellow|Life Fellow]] of the college until his death in 2012.<ref name="obituary"/>

==Awards and honours==
Professor Gray's career was garlanded with many academic honours, including election as a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] (FRS) in 1977.  Gray was awarded an Honorary [[Doctor of Science|DSc]] by the [[University of Leeds]] in 1997.<ref>[http://www.leeds.ac.uk/forstaff/news/article/3285/professor_peter_gray Professor Peter Gray leeds.ac.uk news article. 15 June 2012.]</ref><ref name=frs/> His nomination reads: {{centred pull quote|Gray's work is notable for its range and diversity. He was the first to measure temperature-position profiles in gaseous systems on the verge of ignition by a very fine thermocouple technique. The results show that [[Hydrazine|N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>]] oxidation is a pure thermal branched-chain explosion and that multiple cool flames in hydrocarbon oxidations are thermokinetic. His theoretical work on these and related systems is well recognised as original and comprehensive. The need to acquire ancillary data for his flame studies led Gray to measure the four principal transport properties of gases and his laboratory is now the foremost in this field in the UK. Inter alia this work has contributed to knowledge of intermolecular potential functions of dissimilar pairs. His work on reactivity and thermo chemistry of alkoxy, aryloxy, alkyl and perfluoro alkyl radicals is classical in importance ad quality and he has also made substantial advances in the chemistry of [[Dinitrogen tetroxide|N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>]] and dissociating vapours, azide thermo-chemistry and lattice energies.<ref name=royal>{{cite web |url=https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=show.tcl&dsqSearch=(RefNo==%27EC%2F1977%2F19%27) |title=EC/1977/19: Gray, Peter |publisher=The Royal Society |archivedate=8 September 2014 |archiveurl=https://archive.today/20140908052702/https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=show.tcl&dsqSearch=(RefNo=='EC/1977/19') |location=London |url-status=dead |df=dmy-all }}</ref>
}}

==Personal life==
With his first wife, Barbara (who was a lecturer in [[Biochemistry]] at the [[University of Leeds]]), Gray had four children; Christine, Andrew, David and Sally.  Following her death in 1992 Gray married his second wife, Rachel, who survived him.<ref name="University of Leeds, Obituary"/> His interests included music, hill walking and classical Russian science and maths.<ref name="caius">[http://www.cai.cam.ac.uk/currentmasterandfellows/petergray Gray, Peter — Natural Sciences (Physical)] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120704150344/http://www.cai.cam.ac.uk/currentmasterandfellows/petergray |date=4 July 2012 }}. University of Cambridge</ref>
